newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Workers share sale not seen hurting CANTV price.
newsitem.headline: Workers share sale not seen hurting CANTV price.

text.p: Venezuelan telephone company CANTV stock should not be dented by the forthcoming sale of employees' shares, analysts said, even though the offering could add 10 percent to the current public float.

With an eye to mopping-up the stock overhang, "Warburgs's and Lehmans are treating the sale as a kind of minor private placement, accompanied by road-shows and buy recommendations," said ABN-AMRO telecoms analyst Christopher de Mattos.
SBC Warburg and Lehman brothers led CANTV's $1 billion global share offering in November last year.
"It's an open guess for the rest although my expectation is that some three percent of the company will be sold," he added.
No firm date has yet been set for the sale, when workers C shares can be converted to tradable D shares, nor if it will be on the New York or Caracas stock exchanges, or both.
But according to the November share prospectus, employees can sell upto 30 percent of their holdings in group-organized offerings every six months between May 1997 and November 1998.
"What's very important is that these are not new shares, so the (sale) is not a dilution," said SBC Warburg analyst Zaine Manekia.

"The stock could even rise on the marketing, although afterwards it may be more dull," he added. The stock has firmed 21 percent since late April. Midday Monday its American Depository Receipts (ADRs) were trading down a hair at $35-3/8.

Employees currently own 10.8 percent of the company in the form of Class C shares, bought in 1991 with generous financing terms at $4.71 per share ($32.97 per ADR) -- a price that puts them in the money.
"My guess is that most pensioners will sell, their savings have been eroded by high inflation," said de Mattos.
"What the workers and bankers are probably figuring out is what should come to the market, given that the current share price should not be impacted," he added.
Another nine percent of the company, currently held by the Venezuelan Investment Fund (FIV) and due to be transferred to workers in the future, will not be included in the sales.

"Although we expect the additional supply of shares to present some stock overhang periodically for the next two years, we believe there should be enough demand to absorb the potential additional supply," said investment house Caspian in a research note.
"Use short term negative issues as a buying opportunity," Caspian added.
